1446-perfect-behavior-a-guide-for-ladies:
Donald Ogden Stewart's parody guide takes the stiff rules of etiquette and turns them gently upside down. Chapters cover courtship, weddings, travel, concerts, dinners, and balls, with drawings by Ralph Barton, and each rule is stated with mock gravity before the joke quietly undoes it.

The humour lies in the gap between perfect form and real life: guests who blunder, hosts who panic, and lovers who follow the book to ruin. Written in the 1920s, it pokes fun at a society clinging to manners while the world changes. It is light, clever, and still easy to enjoy.
18514-the-black-sealed-letter-or-the-mis:
Andrew Learmont Spedon printed this Canadian tale at Montreal in 1872. Its hero is a Canadian abroad in London, and its title points to a black-sealed letter at the heart of his troubles. The story opens on a foggy November evening in 1869, among crowded shops, coffee houses, and gin shops, with wealth and want side by side.

Spedon, known for Canadian summer tales and verse, writes in a warm, moral tone, pausing to sketch city life in detail. The plot follows its hero through London streets and setbacks as one small cause shifts his whole life. Readers get both a period melodrama and a picture of Victorian London.
21354-menhardoc:
George Manville Fenn brings Mr Temple and his twin sons to a Cornish fishing village for the summer. Arthur and Richard are the twins in this tale of nets and mines. The twins differ sharply: Arthur, called Taff, is foppish and hates getting wet, while Dick dives into everything going. Local boy Will Marion, clever and well schooled in Latin and Greek, shames Arthur's pride.

Boating trips teach the boys the working life of a Cornish fishing village around 1850, with Josh and Uncle Abram rounding out the cast. The name Menhardoc never appears in the text at all, Fenn's transcriber notes, yet its Cornish sound does the work of a title.
2287-havoc:
E. Phillips Oppenheim, the prince of Edwardian thriller writers, builds Havoc around spies, secrets, and a Europe sliding toward war. A quiet Englishman is drawn into a web of agents and stolen plans, where every dinner guest may be an enemy and every journey a trap. Oppenheim's machinery runs smoothly: clues, chases, and a heroine in danger.

The novel's charm lies in its period atmosphere of hotels, trains, and embassies before the First World War. Readers who enjoy early spy fiction will find the formula already polished here. It is light, fast, and unabashedly entertaining.
23304-the-lady-doc:
Caroline Lockhart wrote this western novel of a lady doctor, released by a New York publisher in the early nineteen teens with a frontispiece by Gayle Hoskins. Dr. Harpe practices in Crowheart, where a rival doctor named Lamb is known chiefly by his card in the local paper.

Chapters on flour gold, fate, and a mesalliance mix medicine with romance and town talk. Lockhart's heroine, like her fighting shepherdess, wins respect in a hard country by skill, nerve, and plain speech. Lockhart's doctor wins respect by skill, nerve, and plain speech in Crowheart. One chapter is called The Humor of the Fate Lachesis, and another, The Church Racket, among Crowheart cases.
5255-the-book-of-good-manners-a-guide-to:
W. C. Green's Book of Good Manners is a dictionary-style guide to polite usage for all social functions in America. Arranged alphabetically for quick reference, it covers accepting or declining invitations, accidents, addresses, afternoon teas, visiting cards, letters of introduction, weddings, and public places, among many other topics.

Green promises a complete and authentic authority on social usage, giving each answer briefly and clearly. The book offers a detailed window into American manners of its day. It still serves readers curious about how their grandparents were expected to behave at table, at tea, and at a wedding.
8819-in-troubadour-land-a-ramble-in-prov:
S. Baring-Gould rambles through Provence and Languedoc in this 1891 travel book, illustrated by J. E. Rogers, with a frontispiece of the tower of St Trophimus at Arles. His epigraph from Tom of Reading in 1600 asks what life is if not mixed with delight, and what delight pleases more than seeing the fashions and manners of unknown places. Baring-Gould insists he is no common gadder, nor one to trouble readers with mere travel.

With Murray, Baedeker, and Guide Joanne already describing antiquities and scenery exactly, he gives instead personal incident: people met, stories heard, and troubadour history felt on the ground. Roman Arles, papal Avignon, and Languedoc towns pass in leisurely chapters. Readers gain a literary traveller's Provence, richer in anecdote than in guidebook fact, and a window onto southern France before mass tourism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-maedoc:
Maedoc, first bishop of Ferns in Wexford, was born about 558 on an island in Brackley Lough, County Cavan. He died on 31 January 626. Son of Sedna, a chieftain of Connacht, and his wife Eithne, he was famed for holiness even in his early years.

When crowds sought to become his disciples, he fled from Ireland to Wales and became a pupil of Saint David, counting as one of his three most faithful disciples. After many years he returned to Ireland with a band of disciples and settled at Brentrocht in Leinster. There he founded several monasteries, the greatest being Ferns, built on land given by Brandubh, king of Leinster, where a synod elected and consecrated him bishop about 598.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-winnoc:
Winnoc, abbot of Wormhout in Flanders, ground corn by miracle in old age, the monks said. Three lives survive, the best written by a monk of St Bertin in the mid-ninth century or a century earlier. Generally called a Breton, he was more probably British, the Bollandist de Smedt argues. He came to St Sithiu, then ruled by Bertin, with three companions.

Soon sent to found Wormhout, a dependent cell or priory, not an abbey as generally called, he ruled there into old age. Enfeebled, he received supernatural help grinding corn for brethren and poor. A curious monk who spied on him was struck blind, then healed by Winnoc's intercession. Many miracles followed his death on 6 November 716 or 717, a year known only from fourteenth-century tradition. His cult spread widely through liturgical books.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-FriendsOfDemocr:
Friends of Democracy issued a short pamphlet titled Henry Ford: Do You Know? in a limited edition priced at ten cents. The pamphlet warns readers about Ford's The International Jew, an antisemitic work in the automaker's name. By the time of the warning, the book was appearing in many languages.

The group charged that Nazi propagandists were distributing Ford's text around the world. A ten-cent pamphlet was the era's cheap weapon against a rich man's printing power. The piece preserves an early American effort to answer hate literature with facts, while the propaganda war was already running.
havoc:
E. Phillips Oppenheim loaded Havoc with the furniture of prewar espionage: crowned heads meeting, a night train from Vienna, and a stolen packet that every spy in Europe wants. Stephen Laverick, an English man of business, is drawn into the game when the packet passes near his hands. Von Behrling carries it, Bellamy hunts it, and Austrian agents multiply around opera houses and supper parties.

Chapters promise robbing the dead, the price of silence, and a partner's flight, and Oppenheim delivers intrigue at a sprint. The stakes are nothing less than war between empires. Oppenheim became the prince of the spy thriller between the wars, and Havoc shows his early formula complete: glamour, treachery, and a civilian learning the great game.
malthus-the-malthusian-herald-devoted-to:
The Malthusian Herald is a penny journal first issued in June 1891. Its subtitle promises a solution of the great social problem. The editor urges readers to limit their families within their means. Letters, he says, pour in from parents at their wits' end.

More children, he argues, means less for those already half provided for. A reprinted discussion on sexual morality fills much of this number. It reports a crowded meeting at Memorial Hall in Farringdon Street. The journal takes its name from Malthus, the population thinker. It campaigned for family limitation decades before that cause won. The paper is a bold relic of Victorian social reform.
perfect-behavior-a-guide-for-ladies-and-: What is hosted here shows only the front matter of Perfect Behavior, the title pages, a mock dedication, and detailed contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Donald Ogden Stewart. It calls the book a guide for ladies and gentlemen in all social crises, and admits it is a parody outline of etiquette, illustrated by Ralph Barton. The contents cover courtship, weddings, travel, concerts, dinners and balls, and etiquette for dry agents.
podcast-dannyjones-58YGzlW3Koc:
Bart Sibrel has argued for decades that the Apollo moon landings were faked. He brings Danny Jones what he calls leaked NASA footage, which he says confirms odd details of the Apollo 11 story. Sibrel walks through the clips and the inconsistencies he believes prove a staged production.

The overwhelming weight of evidence supports the landings as real, and Sibrel's claims have been answered point by point for years. This episode preserves his presentation anyway, because the moon-hoax argument is a durable piece of American folklore and Sibrel is its best-known living advocate. Jones questions him as a host rather than a prosecutor. Listeners get the conspiracy case in its maker's own words, to accept, reject, or simply understand as a cultural artifact.
podcast-joerogan-r4wQsmAtZoc:
Physicist Brian Greene explains the deep structure of the universe in episode 1428 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Greene, a Columbia professor, wrote The Elegant Universe and became a leading public voice for string theory. He is known for making hard physics clear to lay readers.

Greene walks Rogan through strings, hidden dimensions, and the fabric of space and time. He uses plain images to show how reality might have more dimensions than we sense. Rogan asks the big questions about beginnings, endings, and free will. The talk gives curious listeners a guided tour of modern cosmology from a master teacher.
podcast-tuckercarlson-eNYrDAhrDoc:
Tucker Carlson names the four great villains of the medical industrial complex in a solo talk. He frames the health system as a machine that gains from sick people. No guest joins him, so the charge is his alone.

Carlson walks through the four powers he blames most and the harm he lays at each door. He argues the group works as one to block cheap cures and guard its cash. He calls on his crowd to see the game for what it is. Listeners get his full case in one place. The library keeps the talk as a record of his stated view.
the-black-sealed-letter-or-the-misfortun:
Andrew Learmont Spedon printed a tale for Canadian homes in Montreal in 1872, at his own expense. Spedon is also named for Canadian Summer Evening Tales and The Canadian Minstrel. A verse warns how a slight cause may change a life, bringing balm or a canker to the soul.

Chapter one begins not in Canada but with old London, praised as a city of cities. Its foundations, the narrator claims, reach back before Roman feet touched Albion. London's statesmen, authors, churches, law, and old buildings are extolled at length. That long praise sets up, by contrast, the misfortunes of a Canadian cockney promised in the title.
the-book-of-good-manners-a-guide-to-poli:
W. C. Green wrote The Book of Good Manners, a guide to polite use at social events in America. The matter is set in A-to-Z form, so a reader can find a point fast and read it in brief. Cross-notes send the reader from one head word to the next, as from Accidents to Street Etiquette.

Early heads deal with how to write to folk. A man's address may be stamped on his paper, but not with both crest and name mark. A man is Mr. James J. Wilson or James J. Wilson, Esq., but not both forms at once. A woman is never given her husband's rank, as in Mrs. Judge Wilson. A woman with her own rank, such as Dr., keeps it in work mail.
